en: Thus have I heard: the Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasutta, the Fourteenth Discourse in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, for a long time I have understood the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus:”
“Greed is a defilement of the mind, hatred is a defilement of the mind, delusion is a defilement of the mind.
Thus, Bhante, do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One:
“Greed is a defilement of the mind, hatred is a defilement of the mind, delusion is a defilement of the mind.”
"And yet, on certain occasions, states of greed still take possession of my mind; states of hatred still take possession of my mind; and states of delusion still take possession of my mind.
Then, venerable sir, it occurs to me:
'What state, indeed, has not been abandoned within me, because of which states of greed still take possession of my mind...'"
“...they persist; states of hatred also persist, taking possession of the mind; states of delusion also persist, taking possession of the mind.
“It is precisely because that state has not been abandoned within you, Mahānāma, that at times states of greed persist, taking possession of your mind;
states of hatred persist, taking possession of your mind; and states of delusion persist, taking possession of your mind.”
"They persist by completely consuming [the mind].
For if that very teaching, Mahānāma, had been abandoned within you, you would not be living at home nor would you enjoy sensual pleasures.
But because that very teaching has not been abandoned within you, Mahānāma, you live at home and enjoy sensual pleasures."
“‘Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger here is greater’— if, Mahānāma,

this has been well seen by a noble disciple with right wisdom as it really is, yet he does not attain rapture and happiness apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states, nor anything more peaceful than that,
then he still does not turn away from sensual pleasures.”
But when, Mahānāma, for a noble disciple it has been well seen with correct wisdom as it really is: “Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair;
the danger here is greater”—and he attains a joy and happiness apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, or something more peaceful than that;
Then he was not drawn back toward sensual pleasures.
Mahānāma, even before my awakening, while I was still an unawakened bodhisatta, this was well seen by me as it really is with correct wisdom:
"Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger here is greater. Thus was it clearly seen by me with correct wisdom, just as it is.
But apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states, I did not attain a joy and happiness more peaceful than that;
therefore, I was not yet free from attachment to sensual pleasures and did not renounce them.
However, Mahānāma, when it occurred to me: "Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger here is greater"—then, in this way, I [understood].

When this had been clearly seen as it really is with correct wisdom, I attained a joy and happiness apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states, or something even more peaceful than that; then,
without hesitation, I renounced sensual pleasures.
And what, Mahānāma, is the gratification in sensual pleasures?
There are these five strands of sensual pleasure, Mahānāma.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … [and so on].
Tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust— these, Mahānāma,
are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
“Mahānāma, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence upon these five cords of sensual pleasure—
this is the gratification in sensual pleasures.
And what, Mahānāma, is the danger in sensual pleasures?”
In this case, Mahānāma, a clansman earns his living by means of some craft—
whether by calculation, accounting, reckoning, agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, archery, service to the king, or any other craft—
exposed to cold, exposed to heat, afflicted by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and oppressed by hunger and thirst.

This too, Mahānāma, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.

If, Mahānāma, those riches do not accrue to that clansman despite his thus exerting himself, striving, and making an effort, he sorrows, suffers, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion, thinking: "Vain indeed was my exertion; fruitless indeed was my effort."

This too, Mahānāma, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering with sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its source, sensual pleasure as its basis, and sensual pleasure itself as its root.

Now, Mahānāma, if wealth is acquired by a clansman who thus exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort, he experiences pain and grief on account of the protection of that wealth: [thinking] "May no one harm me... and so forth.
‘How can it be that kings do not carry off my wealth, nor thieves steal it, nor fire burn it, nor water sweep it away, nor unloved heirs take it?
Yet, despite guarding and protecting it in this way, those very riches are carried off by kings, or stolen by thieves, or burned by fire, or swept away by water, or taken by unloved heirs.
He grieves, suffers, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion, crying out:
‘Even that which was mine is no longer mine.

This too, Mahānāma, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, it is because of sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as their very cause, that kings [fight with kings].
Kings dispute with kings; kṣatriyas dispute with kṣatriyas; brahmins dispute with brahmins;
householders dispute with householders; even a mother disputes with her son, and a son disputes with his mother;
even a father disputes with his son, and a son disputes with his father; even a brother disputes with a brother, and a brother [disputes with a brother].
A sister quarrels with her brother, and a brother quarrels with his sister; a companion quarrels with his companion.
Having fallen into such strife, contention, and dispute, they attack one another with their hands, they attack with clods of earth, they attack with sticks, and they attack with weapons.
Therein, they undergo even death or suffering equal to death.
This too, Mahānāma, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures,

with sensual pleasures alone as its cause. Furthermore, Mahānāma, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures alone as their cause,
people take up sword and shield, fasten on their bows and quivers, and charge into battle arrayed on both sides, even while arrows are being hurled.
While spears are being hurled and swords are flashing,
they are pierced there by spears, pierced by javelins, and their heads are cut off by swords.
There they meet with death, or with suffering equal to death.
This too, Mahānāma, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures,

and having sensual pleasures as its very cause. Furthermore, Mahānāma, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as their very cause,
people take up swords and shields, fasten on their bows and quivers, and with their bodies smeared with fat, they charge forward as arrows are being shot.
While spears are being hurled and swords are flashing,
they are pierced there by spears, pierced by javelins, drenched with boiling cow dung, crushed by mallets, and their heads are cut off with swords.
There they meet death, or suffering equal to death.
This too, Mahānāma, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures,

with sensual pleasures as its very cause. Furthermore, Mahānāma, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as their very cause,
people cut through embankments, carry off plunder, commit robbery in solitary houses, lie in wait on highways, and go unto the wives of others.
Having seized him, kings inflict various punishments upon him:
they flog him with whips, they flog him with canes, they flog him with clubs;
they cut off his hand, they cut off his foot, they cut off both his hands and feet, they cut off his ear, they cut off his nose.
They cut off their ears; they make them undergo the *bilaṅgathālika* torture, the *saṅkhamuṇḍika* torture,
the *rāhumukha* torture, the *jotimālika* torture, the *hatthapajjotika* torture, the *erakavattika* torture,
the *cīrakavāsika* torture, the *eṇeyyaka* torture, the *baḷisamaṁsika* torture, and the *kahāpaṇika* torture.
They subject them to the "salt-scratch" torture; they subject them to the "rolling-pin" torture; they subject them to the "bed of straw" torture;
they douse them with boiling oil; they have them devoured by dogs; they impale them alive on stakes;
and they cut off their heads with swords.
There they undergo even death, or suffering equal to death.

This too, Mahānāma, is a visible danger regarding sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, on account of sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as their root, with sensual pleasures as their basis, and having sensual pleasures as their very cause, people engage in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having practiced misconduct by body, having practiced misconduct by speech, and having practiced misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.

This too, Mahānāma, is a danger regarding sensual pleasures in the future life—a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.
On one occasion, Mahānāma, I was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.

Now at that time, Mahānāma, a number of Nigaṇṭhas were on the Black Rock on the slope of Isigili, standing in the "upward-standing" posture, having renounced seats, and experiencing painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations resulting from their self-inflicted asceticism.
Then, Mahānāma, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, I went to the Black Rock on the slope of Isigili where those Nigaṇṭhas were; having approached them, I said this to those Nigaṇṭhas:
“‘But, friends Nigaṇṭhas, why do you stand with arms upraised, rejecting seats, and experience painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations?
When this was said, Mahānāma, those Nigaṇṭhas said this to me:
‘Friend, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is omniscient and all-seeing; he claims a knowledge and vision that is entirely complete:’”
“Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously established before me.
He said this:
“Nigaṇṭhas, you have indeed committed evil deeds in the past; wear them away by means of this bitter practice of austerities.”
"But that which is here now—restraint in body, restraint in speech, and restraint in mind—is the non-doing of evil deeds in the future.
Thus, through the wearing away of old kamma by means of austerity and the non-doing of new kamma, there is no further influx in the future.

With no further influx in the future, there is the destruction of kamma; with the destruction of kamma, the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering, the destruction of feeling; and with the destruction of feeling, all suffering will be utterly worn away."
"And that indeed pleases us and is acceptable to us; therefore we are satisfied.
When this was said, Mahānāma, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas:
"But do you, friends Nigaṇṭhas, know—"
‘Did we exist in the past, or did we not exist?
‘No indeed, friend.
‘But then, friends Nigaṇṭhas, do you know:’
‘Did we not ourselves previously perform evil kamma, and did we not refrain from performing it?
‘Certainly not, friend.
‘But then, friends Nigaṇṭhas, do you know—’
‘Did we perform such and such an evil deed?
‘No indeed, friend.
‘But then, friends Nigaṇṭhas, do you know:’
‘Has so much suffering been worn away, or so much suffering remains to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away will all suffering have been worn away?
‘No indeed, friend.
‘But then, friends Nigaṇṭhas, do you know:’
‘The abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states in this very life’?
“Certainly not, friend.
“So it seems, friends Nigaṇṭhas, that you do not know—”
"You did not know: 'We indeed existed in the past, we did not not exist';
you did not know: 'We indeed performed evil kamma in the past, we did not not perform it';
you did not know: 'We performed such and such evil kamma.'"
"Such an amount of suffering has been worn away, such an amount of suffering remains to be worn away, or when such an amount of suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away.
You do not know the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states in this very life.
“If that were so, friend Nigaṇṭhas, those in the world who are cruel, blood-stained, and of harsh deeds, having been reborn among humans, would go forth among the Nigaṇṭhas?
“Friend Gotama, happiness is not to be attained through happiness; rather, happiness is to be attained through suffering.

For if, friend Gotama, happiness were to be attained through happiness, then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would have attained happiness, and King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would be living in greater happiness than the venerable Gotama.”
“Surely, venerable ones, the Nigaṇṭhas have spoken these words hastily and without reflection:
‘Friend Gotama, happiness is not to be attained through happiness; rather, happiness is to be attained through suffering.

If, friend Gotama, happiness were to be attained through happiness, then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would have attained happiness, for King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha dwells in greater happiness than the venerable Gotama.’”
Moreover, I myself should be questioned on this:
"Which of you, venerable sirs, dwells more happily—the Māgadhan King Seniya Bimbisāra, or the venerable Gotama?
Indeed, friend Gotama, we spoke hastily and without reflection. Happiness is not to be attained through happiness; rather, happiness is to be attained through suffering.

"Friend Gotama, if happiness were easily attained, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would have attained it; King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would dwell in greater happiness than the Venerable Gotama.
But setting that aside, we now ask the Venerable Gotama this:
'Who dwells in greater happiness, the King of Magadha Seniya Bimbisāra, or the Venerable Gotama?'"
"Therefore, friends Nigaṇṭhas, I shall question you on this matter; answer as you see fit.

What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas: is King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha able, without moving his body and without uttering a word, to dwell experiencing exclusive happiness for seven days and nights?"

‘No, friend. ‘What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas? Is the Magadhan King Seniya Bimbisāra able, without moving his body or uttering a word, [to cause it to rain] for six days and nights...?’... [as before] ...‘No, friend. ‘What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas? Is the Magadhan King Seniya Bimbisāra able, without moving his body or uttering a word, [to cause it to rain] for six days and nights...?’... For five days and nights...
for four days and nights...
for three days and nights...
‘... for two days and nights ...
or for one day and night to dwell experiencing exclusive happiness?
‘Certainly not, friend.’
“Friends, Nigaṇṭhas, I am indeed able, without moving my body and without uttering speech, to dwell experiencing exclusive happiness for one day and night.
Friends, Nigaṇṭhas, I am indeed able, without moving my body and without uttering speech, to dwell [experiencing exclusive happiness] for two days and nights… for three days and nights…”
four days and nights … five days and nights … six days and nights …
“...to dwell experiencing exclusive happiness for seven days and nights.
What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas, this being so, who dwells more happily: the Māgadha King Seniya Bimbisāra, or I?
“This being so, venerable Gotama, you indeed dwell more happily than King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, Mahānāma the Sakyan rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta, the fourth, is finished.
